prompt:
Use case: precise-object-edit with identity preservation.
Make only the large monitor and its contents fully frontal. Output one 1536x1024 image.

Reference 1 is Demir's canonical portrait. Reference 2 is the Bridge room master. Reference 3 is the current repaired composition, the edit target.

Preserve exactly the target's corrected Demir proportions: same naturally sized head, lean torso, sloping shoulders, neck, arms, two hands, hair, face, expression, charcoal uniform, chair, lap, legs, keyboard action and cartridge grip. Preserve the surrounding Bridge, desk and lighting. Do not re-enlarge the body, hands or head.

The entire monitor FRONT MUST BE A TRUE RECTANGLE parallel to the camera sensor. Fix the remaining shallow tilt of its top edge. Both top and bottom bezel edges must be perfectly horizontal, and both side edges perfectly vertical. The glass inner border must also be exactly rectangular with its top and bottom level. Its four corners should be approximately (920,225), (1480,225), (1480,660), (920,660). No trapezoidal front bezel, no sloping upper glass edge. The existing swivel pedestal supports this frontal orientation. The cartridge slot remains accessible on the monitor's left outer edge, preserving the hand grip exactly.

Keep every title, divider, box edge, arrow and text baseline on this same frontal plane: horizontal baselines and horizontal/vertical box edges. Retain the same large readable task content, precise values and roomy layout. Use these exact labels:
"Practice task"
"Input"
"[[1,2],[3,4]]"
"shape [2,2]"
"Dense:"
"3 units"
"Expected shape"
"[2,3]"
"Single reading"
"[5,6]"
"Add one batch axis"
"Awaiting code"

Keep the upper flow Input to Dense to Expected shape and the separate lower Single reading to Add one batch axis flow. Exactly the same task, no numeric predicted outputs and no completion tick. Demir remains on the visible front side of the screen.

The only change is the monitor's perfectly frontal rectangular geometry and its matching content plane. Preserve all corrected anatomy and the natural hopeful, focused expression.

facts: Challenge follows the failed demo and asks the learner to run a supplied batch and add a batch axis to one flat reading.
The exercise is distinct from the three-feature narrative model.
One dense layer has 3 units and inputShape [2]. Expected output shape is [2,3].
The supplied single reading is [5.0,6.0]. Add one leading batch axis while preserving values.
Random initial weights do not establish prediction accuracy. The challenge image must keep results pending.

attempts.prompt:
Use case: identity-preserve.
Asset type: one finished 1536x1024 landscape Deep Orbit lesson scene, Forward Pass challenge.

Reference images in this exact order:
1. Ensign Demir's canonical neutral portrait is the fixed identity authority.
2. The Bridge master defines room architecture and materials.
3. The current Forward Pass challenge is the edit target and task-content reference.

Primary correction: rebuild Demir's seated upper body, shoulders, neck, arms and chair as one naturally proportioned young adult. The target's giant torso, broad shoulders and oversized foreground arm make his head look too small. Reduce this inflated body mass and extreme foreshortening. Keep his canonical head at a normal adult scale instead of enlarging it into a bobblehead. Use a lean average young-adult build, comfortably sloping shoulders, a normal neck emerging between them, ordinary upper-arm thickness and hands proportional to his face. At comparable depth the shoulders should read around two to two-and-a-half head widths, with perspective allowed, not the huge padded body in the target. Preserve the canonical face width, jaw, chin, nose, eye spacing, brown eyes, freckles, swept dark hair, stubble, ear device and charcoal uniform from image 1.

Candid action: seated at the Bridge workstation after the failed demo, Demir has a small focused, hopeful smile and looks toward the practice display. His left hand holds a small plain rectangular data cartridge beside its visible reader slot, with a relaxed grip and neutral wrist. His right index finger presses one keyboard key while the other fingers curl naturally. Show a separate traceable shoulder, upper arm, elbow, forearm and wrist for each arm. Keep the cartridge and hands at ordinary scale. His chair supports his pelvis and back, with believable desk clearance, lap and thigh placement. Use a calm medium three-quarter camera position with less wide-angle exaggeration. Keep his head, neck and torso aligned with the work.

Display geometry is mandatory: use a large shared monitor on the right on a plausible swivel support. Its complete front bezel and glass are frontal rectangles parallel to the camera sensor. Top and bottom edges are level and left and right edges are vertical. The title, all boxes, arrows, dividers and text baselines share that exact horizontal/vertical plane. Demir and the camera are both on the visible front side, and his gaze reaches the displayed task. Show all four glass corners with generous margins. Use available space for the main task text, large enough to read at 768x512.

Exact display content, preserving the exercise:
Title: "Practice task"
Upper row has three boxes with arrows from left to right:
Box 1: "Input", "[[1,2],[3,4]]", "shape [2,2]"
Box 2: "Dense:", "3 units"
Box 3: "Expected shape", "[2,3]"
A separate lower row has:
"Single reading", "[5,6]" then an arrow to "Add one batch axis".
Footer: "Awaiting code".
No predicted numeric output, completed result or success tick. These are the supplied practice data and expected shapes before the learner runs code.

Preserve the Bridge, warm practical light, muted green interface and aged brass palette, the cartridge action and engaged expression. Other screens stay quiet dark glass. No new people, pointer or paper. Avoid muscular or swollen shoulders, tiny-head proportions, oversized hands, a long thin neck, a bobblehead, twisted grips, duplicate limbs, screen-plane mismatch, clipped labels or camera-facing presentation pose.
